title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + a deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs were analysed after preregistered exclusions. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair was invoked for 6 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not recorded in per‑task artifacts and thus could not be evaluated. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We present preregistered design details, deterministic validator semantics, complete numeric outcomes, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, contamination findings (no exact public duplicates flagged), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and implications.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are actively explored for NetOps tasks such as intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1,2]. Stochastic generation can produce syntactic or semantic violations—missing commands, unsafe operation orderings, or constraint breaches—that create operational risk when applied to device CLIs. To mitigate such risk, research and prototype pipelines propose interposing deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish or header‑space analyses) and bounded repair loops—generate–verify–repair (GVR)—so that only outputs passing a deterministic oracle are considered safe to apply [3–5]. Prior work has described components and small prototypes, but preregistered, paired evaluations that instrument verifier‑triggered repair benefit with archived deterministic traces are limited [1–4].

Motivated by this gap, we asked the preregistered question: Does a GVR pipeline that uses a single sampled initial LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), a deterministic Batfish‑style validator, and at most one automated LLM repair call reduce verifier‑detected semantic/safety failures relative to the same initial candidate without repair? Our principal contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation executed under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher constraints. We preserve the exact preregistered estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), report exact execution accounting and paired contingency counts, provide representative before/after artifacts, and discuss statistical interpretation and validity threats specific to shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.related_work:
LLM applications in NetOps include intent→CLI translation systems and focused benchmarks that study automated configuration synthesis and correctness [1]. Surveys and tutorials summarize opportunities and failure modes for LLMs in network operations and AIOps and advocate verification/grounding components when moving toward automation [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed in code generation and regulated domains to produce deterministic validation guarantees via external oracles and bounded repair loops [3]. Network verification tools such as Batfish and header‑space analyses are natural verifier choices because they enable deterministic reachability and ordering checks over a network model; prior work documents Batfish’s design and verification primitives and motivates its use in LLM‑augmented NetOps prototypes [4]. Analyses of what LLMs require to synthesize correct router configurations emphasize sequencing and vendor‑syntax difficulties, supporting verifier augmentation [5].

Our study differs by executing a preregistered paired test that (a) uses shared_initial_candidate semantics per the preregistration, (b) archives raw model traces and deterministic validator traces for auditability, and (c) reports paired contingency counts and exact tests consistent with the registered analysis plan.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study preregistration is cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under those semantics the same single sampled initial model candidate is used to compute both the baseline outcome (single‑shot candidate → deterministic validator pass/fail) and the guarded outcome (same candidate → verifier; if it fails, at most one automated LLM repair is permitted; final verifier pass/fail recorded). This paired design isolates the effect of the allowed validator‑triggered repair step for a fixed initial candidate.

Task bank and sampling: The preregistered task bank deterministically produced 300 intent→CLI pairs (150 Cisco‑like; 150 Juniper‑like) using a deterministic synthetic task generator combined with public NetConfEval‑style examples; generation seeds, generator id, and per‑task manifest entries are archived. Inclusion/exclusion, retry, and missingness rules followed the preregistration. Deterministic exclusion logic removed 34 both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures (documented in analysis/missingness_summary.csv), leaving 266 complete paired units for the primary analysis (complete_pairs = 266).

Model, orchestration, and sampling disclosure: The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Archived configuration fields include max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset). The archived null temperature value does not prove deterministic sampling (temperature=0); no deterministic sampling seed was archived and model provider call accounting indicates hosted_model_call_event_count = 306 with 34 failed calls. The orchestration adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and stage accounting recorded shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6 (six repair calls observed). These execution metadata are used below in failure accounting and reproducibility notes.

Deterministic validator semantics: The experiment used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the binary oracle. The validator executes: CLI syntactic parsing and normalization, per‑task required‑sequence checks (expected_sequence vs parsed commands), constrained‑field touch checks (allowed_fields and allowed_touched_fields), and reachability/constraint validation on the synthetic topology model. Each episode record archives validation_before and validation_after traces, including parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, and a normalized_configuration string. The validator’s outcome is the binary pass/fail used for the primary endpoint and is available per episode in execution/scoring/*.json artifacts.

Repair loop and shared_initial_candidate mechanics: Per the preregistration the initial sampled candidate is shared across baseline and guarded outcomes (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). If the deterministic validator fails that candidate, the guarded arm may invoke at most one automated LLM repair call. Repairs are bounded: the repair prompt exposes the validator’s failure codes and task constraints and requests a corrected configuration; repair prompts and provider traces are archived when invoked. The design choice (≤1 repair) was preregistered to capture a constrained human‑analog escalation where only a single automated correction is permitted before escalation or human review.

Analysis plan and inferential methods: The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (α=0.05). For interval estimation we preregistered a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the paired difference; both procedures were executed by the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. The bootstrap CI was included to quantify paired‑difference magnitude and uncertainty in finite samples; because exact McNemar uses only discordant counts and produces discrete p‑values, reporting both inferential perspectives aids interpretation in small‑discordant settings (see Results). Secondary estimands included median_repair_iterations_per_task and preregistered median end‑to‑end latency (the latter could not be evaluated because latency was not recorded per episode). Missingness handling followed the preregistered plan (complete_pair_primary): 34 both‑arm provider failures were excluded from the primary analysis; sensitivity analyses treated those as failures to check robustness.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and failures: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68. Complete paired units analysed = 266; both_missing_pairs = 34 were excluded per preregistration (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider and model call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, cache_hit_count = 0, and cache_miss_count = 272. Repair stage calls recorded = 6 (repair stage_count = 6). The reconciliation artifact confirms stage accounting and that cross‑condition cache reuse did not occur.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (complete_pairs = 266): baseline successes = 260; guarded final successes = 265. Paired contingency counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 260 (both pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed proportions: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015. Paired difference = 0.01879699248. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered α=0.05 decision rule → not significant). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601] (analysis_log.jsonl contains bootstrap parameters and seed). The bootstrap CI narrowly excludes zero while the exact McNemar test does not reject at α=0.05; this pattern is expected in small‑discordant samples because exact McNemar p‑values are discrete and depend only on discordant counts (here n10=5, n01=0), whereas bootstrap CIs summarize empirical paired‑difference variability across resamples.

Repair behavior and representative artifacts: Repair was invoked 6 times across the planned 300 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0 (H2(a) confirmed). Representative artifact example: task‑000008 (execution/responses/task-000008-shared-initial.txt, sha256 = 89306095...) shows the shared initial candidate terminated with an incomplete final line "interface uplink2\n" and produced an invalid/incomplete configuration (validation_before showed parsed_command_count mismatch). The guarded final artifact (execution/responses/task-000008-guarded.txt, sha256 = d52b7616f...) contains the corrected complete sequence including "interface uplink2 admin down" and the subsequent edge1 commands; its validator trace shows validation_after passing. All episode validator traces (execution/scoring/task-000008-*.json) show the concrete failure codes that triggered repair and the normalized_configuration that the validator accepted after repair.

Contamination and sensitivity checks: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty—no exact public‑duplicate tasks were flagged and none were excluded for contamination in the primary analysis. Sensitivity treating the 34 excluded both‑arm episodes as failures (conservative N=300 analysis) yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333 with the same discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0) and exact McNemar p = 0.0625, confirming that the primary inferential conclusion is robust to the preregistered conservative missingness handling.

Supplementary quantitative accounting (archived artifacts): condition_summary.csv and paired_contingency_table.csv are archived (their SHA‑256 values are in analysis artifact hashes). The deterministic_reconciliation.json documents that all deterministic consistency checks passed and provides provider call and stage counts used above.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The guarded GVR pipeline produced a small absolute increase in validator pass‑rate (~1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The apparent tension with the bootstrap CI that excludes zero illustrates finite‑sample discreteness: McNemar’s test depends solely on discordant counts while bootstrap CIs reflect resampled paired‑difference variability and can exclude zero in small‑discordant contexts. We therefore present both inferential perspectives to allow readers to judge practical relevance versus formal hypothesis acceptance.

Operational implications and boundary conditions: The marginal benefit of the bounded automated repair was limited because baseline single‑shot pass rate was already high (≈97.7%), leaving few failures for repair to correct. Repair invocations were rare (6/300), suggesting that for this task corpus and model most single‑shot samples satisfied the deterministic validator. These data imply that for high‑first‑pass accuracy workloads, the operational ROI of adding an automated bounded repair stage may be small; conversely, GVR may yield larger gains when first‑pass accuracy is lower or verifier coverage is expanded.

Threats to validity (detailed): Internal validity: our shared_initial_candidate estimand measures the effect of validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent multiple draws or constrained first‑pass prompting (those alternatives were not executed under the preregistration and thus are outside the estimand). Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a predefined set of syntactic, required‑sequence, and reachability rules; semantic violations outside its rule battery are undetected and unmeasured. External validity: tasks derive from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results may not generalize to other vendors, larger production topologies, or workloads with different baseline difficulty distributions. Conclusion validity: few discordant pairs (n10=5, n01=0) and the loss of 34 provider‑failure pairs reduced power and precision; future studies should plan for higher discordant counts or larger N when baseline pass rates are expected to be high.

Design lessons and recommendations: (1) When baseline pass rates are high, prioritize experiments on lower‑baseline task corpora to better quantify repair effectiveness. (2) Record per‑episode latency and pipeline timing to evaluate preregistered operational bounds (the preregistered H2(b) could not be evaluated because latency was not archived). (3) Expand and document validator coverage to reduce construct‑validity uncertainty and to measure false negatives of the verifier itself. (4) Consider experimental designs that contrast shared_initial_candidate semantics with independent multiple draws or constrained prompting in separate preregistered arms (explicitly preregistering those alternative estimands).
sections.conclusion:
A preregistered paired experiment evaluated a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) on intent→CLI tasks under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved validator pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be assessed. All execution and analysis artifacts, including raw responses, validator traces, provider call accounting, and reconciliation manifests, are archived in the evidence bundle to support reanalysis and follow‑on work.

[1] C. Wang, M. Scazzariello, A. Farshin, S. Ferlin, D. Kostić, and M. Chiesa, “NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration?,” in Proc. ACM, 2024. DOI: 10.1145/3656296.
[2] S. Y. Long, J. Tan, B. Mao, F. Tang, Y. Li, M. Zhao, and N. Kato, “A Survey on Intelligent Network Operations and Performance Optimization Based on Large Language Models,” IEEE Commun. Surveys & Tutorials, 2025. DOI: 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606.
[3] R. Cadenas, “Convergent Correctness in Stochastic Code Generation: A Generate‑Verify‑Repair Architecture for Deterministic Validation of Autonomous AI Coding Agents in Regulated Environments,” SSRN, 2026. DOI: 10.2139/ssrn.6754899.
[4] M. Brown, A. Fogel, D. Halperin, V. Heorhiadi, R. Mahajan, and T. Millstein, “Lessons from the evolution of the Batfish configuration analysis tool,” Proc., 2023. DOI: 10.1145/3603269.3604866.
[5] R. Mondal, A. Tang, R. Beckett, T. Millstein, and G. Varghese, “What do LLMs need to Synthesize Correct Router Configurations?,” Proc., 2023. DOI: 10.1145/3626111.3628194.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
